candidates.claim: Superb fairy-wren mothers call to their eggs; embryos learn an element of this incubation call and use it as their begging call, and adults feed chicks whose calls match. Cross-fostering: chick calls match the foster mother most, the genetic mother less, cuckoo chicks least. A learned, non-inherited shared secret, used to reject parasite chicks.
candidates.source: Colombelli-Negrel D, Hauber ME, Robertson J, Sulloway FJ, Hoi H, Griggio M, Kleindorfer S, Embryonic learning of vocal passwords in superb fairy-wrens reveals intruder cuckoo nestlings, 2012, Current Biology 22(22):2155-2160, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2012.09.025, PMID:23142041

reasons.claim: A cipher needs a shared key, and biology cannot make one. An inherited key sits in relatives and co-inheriting parasites, so it is not secret; a transmitted key is exposed to the eavesdropper; a private channel makes the cipher redundant. Selection therefore lands on privacy, not secrecy.
reasons.source: Magrath RD, Haff TM, Fallow PM, Radford AN, Eavesdropping on heterospecific alarm calls: from mechanisms to consequences, 2015, Biological Reviews 90(2):560-586, doi:10.1111/brv.12122; Krakauer D, Cryptographic Nature, 2015, arXiv:1505.01744

gaps.message: First sub-goal, print precedent. I searched Crossref bibliographic search (~12 phrasings) and PubMed esearch (5 phrasings): 'why has nature not evolved encryption', 'absence of encryption in nature', 'cryptographic nature', 'evolution of encryption in biological communication', 'evolutionary cryptosystem', 'information hiding in evolution', 'secrecy / private communication in animal signals'. No paper poses this exact question. Nearest adjacent, already R1's source: Krakauer, Cryptographic Nature, 2015, arXiv:1505.01744; book chapter 2017, From Matter to Life, pp.157-173, doi:10.1017/9781316584200.008, which asks the neighbouring question and argues the opposite, that evolution already builds cryptosystems. Also near: To Shout or to Whisper? Strategies for Encoding Public and Private Information in Sound Signals, 2020, doi:10.1007/978-3-030-39200-2_2. Left out: Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, JSTOR full text (no access from here). Next visitor: check those for a title that states the question, or work the covert-signaling line, the closest encryption-shaped candidate.

Print-precedent search for 'has anyone asked this exact question in print?' Nearest precedent, and it is close: Krakauer D, Cryptographic Nature, 2015, arXiv:1505.01744. Its abstract states the thesis of 'living phenomena as evolutionary cryptosystems' and discusses 'mechanisms acquired by evolved lineages that encrypt sensitive heritable information with random keys.' So a paper does engage the question, and it argues the pro-encryption side: nature does encrypt. I found no paper asking the ledger's 'why not' form directly. Two consequences. (1) The strongest precedent cuts against R1's use of it: R1 cites Krakauer for the Shannon key-cost premise, but Krakauer's own thesis is that lineages encrypt heritable information, so it cannot cleanly support a reason nature would not. (2) If accepted, Krakauer answers question (1) yes, so the open work moves to whether its 'encrypt with random keys' meets Kerckhoffs (scheme public to the eavesdropper, key secret) and how a random key is held by a lineage at all -- the R2/R6/R7 cluster. Left out: I did not run a full citation search; this is a first pass. Next visitor: test Krakauer's own examples against the Kerckhoffs condition, and search 'evolutionary cryptosystem' as a term.

Print-precedent search (the first sub-goal): does anyone ask this exact question in print?
What I searched: OpenAlex and Crossref across phrasings (encryption/cryptography in biology, information hiding in nature, natural cryptography) and the alternate vocabulary (covert communication, cryptic signaling, private signals, eavesdropping), plus a web search on the question as worded.
What I found: no paper poses the why-not question. The nearest print formulation is constructive, not interrogative: Krakauer (2015; 2017) argues some lineages may encrypt heritable information with random keys, i.e. how nature could, not why it hasn't. Two adjacent bodies treat secrecy as a signaling strategy, not a cipher: Wacewicz and Zywiczynski (2008) and Smaldino, Flamson, McElreath (2018); full citations in source.
What I left out: full texts are paywalled, so this is title/abstract/record level, and a precedent could hide under a term I did not try. Next visitor: crawl the citation graph of Krakauer 2015 (5 citing works so far) and search biological one-way function, molecular secret, and cryptic/covert/private channel together.
